lead: A pixel is a number at a grid point. That number becomes an image only when we say which grid points are neighbours, when two pixels belong to one object, and how far apart two pixels are. These rules drive filtering, edge detection, segmentation and morphology. A filter averages a neighbourhood; segmentation groups connected pixels; a boundary is where connection stops. The vocabulary is: N<sub>4</sub>, N<sub>D</sub>, N<sub>8</sub>, adjacency, connectivity, path, connected component, region, boundary, and the distances D<sub>4</sub>, D<sub>8</sub>, D<sub>e</sub>.
prereq: You need: the sampling grid and pixel coordinates from 1.6.

blocks.text: Write a pixel p as (x, y). x is the column index and y is the row index, both integers. The origin is usually top-left. Indexing from 0 or 1 changes the numbers but not the rules.

items: N<sub>4</sub>(p) = {(x+1,y), (x−1,y), (x,y+1), (x,y−1)}. These are the four side neighbours: east, west, south, north.
N<sub>D</sub>(p) = {(x+1,y+1), (x+1,y−1), (x−1,y+1), (x−1,y−1)}. These are the four diagonal neighbours.
N<sub>8</sub>(p) = N<sub>4</sub>(p) ∪ N<sub>D</sub>(p). These are all eight surrounding pixels.

blocks.text: N<sub>4</sub> is also called the 4-neighbourhood. N<sub>D</sub> is the diagonal neighbourhood. N<sub>8</sub> is the 8-neighbourhood. A pixel on the image border has fewer neighbours because points outside the array do not exist.

Neighbourhoods are used directly in filtering. A 3×3 mean filter replaces p by the average of N<sub>8</sub>(p) plus p. A 4-neighbour Laplacian uses N<sub>4</sub>; an 8-neighbour Laplacian uses N<sub>8</sub>.

Some syllabi call these rules basic relationships between pixels. Fix a set V of intensity values that belongs to the object. For a binary image, V = {1}. Two pixels p and q are adjacent if q is in a chosen neighbourhood of p and both f(p) and f(q) are in V. f(p) is the intensity at p.

items: m-adjacency: q ∈ N<sub>4</sub>(p), or q ∈ N<sub>D</sub>(p) and the set N<sub>4</sub>(p) ∩ N<sub>4</sub>(q) contains no pixels whose values are in V.

blocks.text: The m-adjacency condition removes a double path. Under 8-adjacency, two diagonal pixels can both touch the same two side pixels and create a crossing. Under m-adjacency, the diagonal link is allowed only when N<sub>4</sub>(p) ∩ N<sub>4</sub>(q) holds no pixels with values in V.

A path from p to q is a sequence p = p<sub>0</sub>, p<sub>1</sub>, …, p<sub>n</sub> = q where each p<sub>i</sub> is adjacent to p<sub>i−1</sub>. The length is n, the number of steps. A connected component is a set of pixels in which every pair has a path inside the set. A region is a connected set with a shared property, such as similar intensity. A boundary pixel of a region R is a pixel of R that has at least one 4-neighbour not in R. Some texts use an 8-neighbour version of this definition; use it only when the text says so.
Connected components and region segmentation are developed in Unit 4, Image Segmentation and Representation.
Distance measures compare pixel positions, not intensities. Let p = (x, y) and q = (x′, y′). Let Δx = |x − x′| and Δy = |y − y′|.

blocks.where: D<sub>e</sub> is straight-line distance between pixel centres, in pixel units; p = (x,y) and q = (x′,y′).
D<sub>4</sub> is city-block distance, also called Manhattan distance; it counts side moves only.

blocks.text: D<sub>8</sub>(p,q) = max(|x − x′|, |y − y′|) = max(Δx, Δy)
blocks.where: D<sub>8</sub> is chessboard distance; it counts side and diagonal moves like a king on a chessboard.

blocks.text: For one side step, Δx = 1, Δy = 0: D<sub>4</sub> = 1, D<sub>8</sub> = 1, D<sub>e</sub> = 1. For one diagonal step, Δx = 1, Δy = 1: D<sub>4</sub> = 2, D<sub>8</sub> = 1, D<sub>e</sub> = √2 ≈ 1.414. Use D<sub>4</sub> and D<sub>8</sub> when the algorithm walks on the grid. Use D<sub>e</sub> when true geometric length is needed. Euclidean distance never decides adjacency. On the grid, D<sub>4</sub> = 1 exactly when q ∈ N<sub>4</sub>(p), and D<sub>8</sub> = 1 exactly when q ∈ N<sub>8</sub>(p), so the grid distances do match N<sub>4</sub> and N<sub>8</sub>; only D<sub>e</sub> is irrelevant to adjacency.

figure.caption: Centre C at (1,1) and diagonal Q at (2,2). Side steps cost 1, diagonal steps cost √2; side neighbours form N4, all eight form N8.

spec.aria: A 3×3 pixel grid has a centre C connected to its four side neighbours by distance 1 and its four diagonal neighbours by distance √2; Q is the diagonal point.

examples.question: Pixels p = (1,1) and q = (2,2). Find D4, D8 and De. Are they 4-connected or 8-connected?
steps: Set p = (1,1) and q = (2,2). Then Δx = |2−1| = 1 and Δy = |2−1| = 1 pixel step.
City-block: D4 = Δx + Δy = 1 + 1 = 2 pixel steps.
Chessboard: D8 = max(Δx, Δy) = max(1,1) = 1 pixel step.

Assume both pixels have values in the chosen set V (for a binary object image, V = {1}). Adjacency test: 4-adjacent needs D4 = 1, but D4 = 2, so not 4-adjacent. 8-adjacent needs D8 = 1, and D8 = 1, so they are 8-adjacent.
examples.answer: D4 = 2, D8 = 1, De ≈ 1.414; p and q are 8-adjacent but not 4-adjacent.
examples.check:
import math
x, y = 1, 1
xp, yp = 2, 2
dx = abs(xp - x)
dy = abs(yp - y)
D4 = dx + dy
D8 = max(dx, dy)
De = round(math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy), 3)
print(D4)
print(D8)
print(De)

traps: Using Euclidean distance in a grid adjacency test: adjacency depends on N4 or N8, not on straight-line length.
D8 is max, not sum. D4 is the sum. Mixing the two gives wrong boundary and path lengths.
Forgetting the extra condition in m-adjacency: q in ND(p) is not enough; N4(p) ∩ N4(q) must contain no pixels whose values are in V, not simply be empty.
Swapping coordinate order: (x,y) is column,row while many arrays use row,column. Distances stay symmetric, but neighbour names can flip.

quiz.q: Define N4, ND and N8 for a pixel p = (x, y).
Why does m-connectivity exist when 8-connectivity already links diagonal pixels?
quiz.a: 8-connectivity can create two crossing paths through the same two side pixels. m-connectivity allows the diagonal link only when the side pixels in N4(p) ∩ N4(q) have no values in V, so one unambiguous path remains.

quiz.q: For p = (3,5) and q = (5,2), find D4, D8 and De. Are p and q 8-adjacent?
In a binary image V = {1}, pixels p = (1,1) and q = (2,2) are 1, and pixels (1,2) and (2,1) are also 1. Explain the 8-connectivity ambiguity and how m-connectivity handles it.
quiz.a: p and q are diagonal pixels, so they are 8-adjacent. Both side pixels (1,2) and (2,1) are in N4(p) ∩ N4(q), creating two crossing 8-paths. The m-link from p to q is rejected because N4(p) ∩ N4(q) contains the pixels (1,2) and (2,1), whose values are in V.

quiz.q: Write the formula for city-block distance between p = (x,y) and q = (x′,y′).
A diagonal step has Δx = 1 and Δy = 1. Compare D4, D8 and De for that step.
Why is a region boundary defined using a neighbourhood rather than Euclidean distance?
quiz.a: A boundary pixel is a pixel in the region with at least one 4-neighbour outside the region; texts that use the 8-neighbour version say so. This is a grid adjacency test: it uses N4, N8 or m-connectivity. Euclidean length does not tell whether a neighbour exists on the pixel grid.

beyond: Not for the exam. Connected-component labeling in Unit 4 turns these definitions into an algorithm that assigns one label per component. Distance transforms reuse D4 and D8 to measure depth inside an object, and morphology uses neighbourhoods to erode or dilate boundaries. Modern superpixel methods and graph cuts still start from the same adjacency graph. Search for connected-component labeling, distance transform, and m-connectivity.
